sections.heading: Remembering who you are as Father and Lord
sections.text: Sovereign Lord, you made every person and keep every life in your hands. In that sense, all of us belong to you. But you are Father in a deeper way to those who know you, love you, and gladly honor you. You bring your children under the good rule of Jesus, where obedience is not slavery but life, and where your commands are not a burden but a gift.
theological_themes: God as Creator and Sustainer of all people
God's special fatherly relationship with those who belong to him
The goodness of Christ's rule and the beauty of obedience

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that God made all people and gives them life and breath, grounding the prayer's confession that every human life depends on God as Creator and Sustainer.
Jesus describes his yoke as easy and his burden as light, which supports the prayer's confidence that life under Christ's lordship is good and not crushing.
John connects love for God with keeping his commandments and insists they are not burdensome, illuminating the prayer's delight in God's commands.

sections.heading: Admitting how poorly I have responded to your goodness
sections.text: Father, I have not let your undeserved kindness change me as it should. I have wasted blessings that should have helped me grow. I have had light, teaching, worship, Scripture, and chances to do good, and I have often treated them casually. I have been slow to serve others and careless with opportunities you gave me. I come to you with my sins in the open. Please have mercy on me, and let your kindness lead me to real repentance.
theological_themes: Confession of sin despite spiritual privilege
Repentance produced by God's kindness, not self-improvement

scripture_references.connection: Paul says God's kindness is meant to lead people to repentance, directly grounding the prayer's request that divine goodness would soften and turn the heart.
This passage holds together the seriousness of sin and the richness of God's mercy, matching the prayer's honest confession and plea for compassion.
James teaches that failing to do the good one knows to do is sin, which supports the prayer's confession of negligence in doing good to others.

sections.heading: Asking you to change how I live
sections.text: Teach me to hate every path that leads away from you, and help me actually leave it. Make me honest about the state of my soul and the kind of person I am becoming. Guard my mouth. Keep my heart awake and careful. Help me watch and pray when temptation is near. Put to death what is sinful in me, and make me deeply concerned for people who do not yet know you.
theological_themes: Turning from sin in concrete areas of life
Concern for the salvation of others

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist's love for God's precepts produces hatred for false ways, supporting the prayer's request for a heart that rejects sin because it has learned God's truth.
The command to keep the heart with vigilance directly illuminates the prayer's desire for inward watchfulness, not merely outward behavior.
James warns that unbridled speech exposes hollow religion, giving biblical weight to the prayer's request for help in governing the tongue.
Jesus tells his disciples to watch and pray so they will not enter temptation, matching the prayer's plea for alert dependence when temptation comes.
Paul commands believers to put sinful earthly desires to death, grounding the prayer's request for the mortification of sin.

sections.heading: Bringing my family to you
sections.text: God, I cannot bear the thought of people I love being lost. The ones bound to me by family affection are precious to me; let them be precious in your sight, and make them wholly yours. Use my prayers, my words, my correction, my example, and the ordinary life of my home for their good. Make my household a place where heaven is taken seriously, where Christ is loved, and where faith is not just spoken about but lived.
theological_themes: Burden for the salvation of family members
Dependence on God to make family ministry fruitful
Household discipleship through prayer, instruction, correction, and example

scripture_references.connection: Paul expresses deep anguish for his own people who are separated from Christ, giving biblical shape to the prayer's grief over kindred who may be lost.
Israel was commanded to teach God's words diligently in ordinary family life, supporting the prayer's desire that home life become a place of spiritual formation.
Joshua's resolve that his household would serve the Lord resonates with the prayer's longing for the home to be devoted to God's glory.

sections.heading: Asking you to make church and home places of lasting fruit
sections.text: Lord, bless your church and make it like a garden you are planting and tending. Raise up people who are rooted in you, full of the righteousness that comes from you, and fruitful for your glory. And please do not let anyone in my family settle for being pleasant, respectable, or admired while still missing eternal life. If your Word has stirred their conscience, softened their heart, frightened them about sin, or delighted them with truth, do not let those beginnings fade away. Carry your work through to victory in everyone I love.
theological_themes: The church as God's cultivated people for his glory
The insufficiency of morality without salvation
Prayer that early spiritual convictions become lasting saving faith

scripture_references.connection: Isaiah describes God's redeemed people as oaks of righteousness planted by the Lord for his glory, closely supporting the prayer's image of a church made fruitful by God's own planting.
Jesus teaches that no one can see the kingdom of God without being born again, grounding the warning that admirable character and moral appearance are not the same as salvation.

Matthew presents Jesus as the servant who does not crush what is bruised but brings justice to victory, illuminating the prayer's hope that fragile spiritual beginnings would be carried through by Christ.
Paul's confidence that God completes the good work he begins supports the prayer's request that early conviction and delight in God's Word would not disappear but mature into lasting faith.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original distinguishes God as Creator-Father of all people from God as the special Father of those who know, love, and honor him. That distinction is biblically supportable but can be pastorally sensitive because 'Father of all' may sound like universal salvation if left unexplained.

The line about family members who are 'amiable, moral, attractive' yet may fall short of heaven reflects a strong evangelical/Puritan concern that outward respectability is not saving faith. This was preserved without implying that kindness or morality are bad in themselves.

The request that God bless domestic 'discipline' is culturally broad and can be misunderstood in a modern context. It was rendered as 'correction' within a larger pattern of prayer, words, example, and ordinary household life, avoiding any endorsement of harsh or abusive practices.

The prayer assumes a person's spiritual responsibility and influence within the household. In a modern setting family structures vary widely, so the adaptation keeps the emphasis on faithful personal witness and dependence on God rather than control over others' faith.
significant_interpretive_choices: 'Religious privileges' was interpreted as concrete access to teaching, worship, Scripture, and opportunities for obedience, rather than as social or institutional status.

'My house may be a nursery for heaven' was rendered as a home where heaven is taken seriously, Christ is loved, and faith is lived, preserving the image of spiritual formation without reproducing the archaic metaphor exactly.
'My church the garden of the Lord' was interpreted as the gathered people of God being planted and made fruitful by him, supported by Isaiah's 'oaks of righteousness' imagery.

'Bring forth judgment unto victory' was read through Matthew 12's language about Christ bringing justice to victory, and applied to the hope that early convictions under the Word would become lasting saving faith rather than temporary religious feeling.
